newsitem.title: SPAIN: Analysts recommend late-97 Argentaria sale.
newsitem.headline: Analysts recommend late-97 Argentaria sale.

text.p: Spain should sell its remaining stake in bank Argentaria as late as possible next year to give new management time to whip the shaken group into shape, analysts suggested on Tuesday.

The five-month-old conservative government announced on Monday a sweeping privatisation plan for 1997 that will see the sale of the state's remaining stakes in Telefonica, Repsol and Argentaria as well as two-thirds of electrical group Endesa.

The government gave no specific schedule for the sale of its 25 percent stake in Argentaria, Spain's third-largest bank, but analysts recommend it hold off until the new management sketches out a clear strategy and the bank begins to profit from it.
"They are certainly going to leave it until the end of the year," said Lola Ybarra, analyst at Banco Santander de Negocios. "The market is waiting for a change of focus -- for a clear strategy."

In the first corporate appointment after its election, the government put Francisco Gonzalez in charge of the bank, replacing the man who had steered it for the five years since it was created from a merger of state-controlled banking interests.
In late September, Gonzalez named Ramon Bustamante, formerly of rival bank Banesto, to the new position of managing director to help transform the bank.
"They are in the middle of a restructuring," a Madrid-based analyst said. "This is a group with many problems...We have to wait for the new management to get settled in.
"We are putting together a possible calendar and we think it could be in the third quarter after Telefonica and Repsol but before Endesa," she said.
The bank has been plagued by margins that have deteriorated more sharply than those of competitors, by poor trading profits and by weaknesses since its inception, analysts said.
In the first six months of the year, earnings fell by an unexpectedly steep 10.7 percent. They are seen remaining poor for the full year.
"I don't see a brilliant short-term future for the group," the Madrid-based analyst said.
Nevertheless, others said that despite the problems they expected the sale to go well.
"I don't think there will be any problem. The best evidence is the last three sales," said Juan Berberana, analyst at AB Asesores.

The most recent sale, of 25 percent in March, went well despite political uncertainty as it coincided with an election that ended 13 years of Socialist rule. The Socialist government, which set up the sale, lost the vote and negotiations to put the new government in place took two months.
"I think it will go well. Things could hardly have been worse the last time around and it went well," said one analyst.
